title: Artificial Intelligence Interventions in Mathematics Education: A Systematic Literature Review
extended_summary:
This paper presents a systematic literature review of empirical studies published from 2020 to 2024 on artificial intelligence interventions in mathematics education. The review asks two main questions: what kinds of AI-based interventions are being used in mathematics classrooms, and what impact these interventions have on student outcomes such as academic performance, engagement, and personalization. The authors position the review as addressing a gap in prior work by focusing specifically on classroom-based mathematics applications rather than broader STEM or theoretical AI-in-education discussions.

The interventions reviewed include intelligent tutoring systems (ITS), adaptive learning platforms, AI-powered educational applications such as Photomath and ChatGPT, and a smaller number of other tools such as AI-supported virtual reality and AI engines for task personalization. Across the 14 included empirical studies, the review synthesizes findings on outcomes including mathematics achievement, problem-solving, engagement, and some teaching-related outcomes. The review follows PRISMA procedures, searched multiple databases, and included both quantitative and qualitative studies.

The reviewed studies span elementary through postsecondary education and were conducted across multiple countries, including the United States, Slovakia, Philippines, Israel, Spain, Nigeria, Argentina, Taiwan, South Korea, Sweden, and Jordan. Most studies focused on students, though some examined teachers or preservice teachers. The instructional context emphasized classroom-integrated AI tools in mathematics domains such as fractions, arithmetic, algebra, and pre-calculus, with intervention durations ranging from very short sessions to a full school year.

The review concludes that AI tools in mathematics education are generally promising, especially ITS and adaptive platforms used over sustained periods and aligned with instructional goals. Larger effects were associated with longer-duration interventions and with tools providing personalized instruction and real-time feedback; for example, Photomath and some adaptive systems showed moderate to large effects. At the same time, the authors stress that impact depends heavily on context, duration, and teacher involvement, and that shorter interventions or poorly integrated tools tend to show smaller or more limited gains. They also highlight ethical issues such as privacy, fairness, transparency, and the continuing importance of teachers in mediating AI use.

finding.finding_summary: In the reviewed randomized controlled trial, ALEKS showed no statistically significant effect on end-of-course algebra exam scores compared with the comparison condition.

In Shin (2022), integration of ITS tools including ALEKS was associated with moderate improvement in prospective teachers’ technological pedagogical content knowledge when the systems were positioned as instructional partners.
Most students benefited from ASSISTments, with 65-71% mastering key skills after initial ITS practice, but some subgroups showed wheel-spinning and needed additional support.
